A smart ring prototype developed by engineers at the University of California appears to have cracked one of the holy grails of health wearables: non-invasive blood glucose measurement. Data is transmitted to a companion app on a paired iPhone.

Current smart rings rely solely on biophysical data extracted from sensors, such as those embedded in the Apple Watch, but this ring can also track chemical biomarkers by analyzing sweat……

Today's smart rings work in exactly the same way as the Apple Watch, using the exact same sensors. These sensors can collect a wide range of data, including resting heart rate, heart rate variability, respiration rate, body temperature, cardiovascular age, activity levels, sleep cycles, and more.

But adding molecular sensors to existing sensors would dramatically expand the amount of health data that can be collected. You don't even need to deliberately break a sweat—according to CNET, the technology can draw sweat from the skin.

Engineers at the University of California, San Diego believe they have created the first smart ring that uses sweat from your finger to track chemical biomarkers. The ring is currently only a prototype, but it has demonstrated the potential for future smart rings to continuously monitor the body at the molecular level, rather than relying solely on biophysical data. In a paper published on July 23 in Nature Communications, the engineering team reported that the new smart ring can continuously monitor up to four of the following biochemical indicators using sweat: glucose, ketones, vitamin C, uric acid, lactate, and alcohol levels.

This ring could be particularly useful for people with Type 1 diabetes.

Test results show its accuracy is very close to that of invasive continuous glucose monitors and blood draws.

The prototype ring is somewhat bulky and has a battery life of just 12 hours, but the commercialized version is expected to make significant improvements in both areas. I'm eager to see how Apple engineers might apply this technology.
